name: Tomas Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Greenway Garage, a small independent place behind the retail park that's moved heavily into hybrids and electric cars. Sofia, the owner, bought the battery testing kit two years ago and now half our work is hybrids that other garages won't touch. I'm the junior, so I do the servicing, the brake fluid, the cabin filters and a lot of fetching. My hands are still slow and I've rounded off more bolts than I'd like to admit, but I'm the one who reads the wiring diagrams fastest because I ask an AI to explain them while I'm standing at the car.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Inês, she's in her second year of nursing, so right now I'm the main wage. We've got about two and a half months of costs saved, which I watch like a hawk. I use AI every day, for work, for budgeting, for planning trips. I'm the person my friends ask to set up their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, the hype got ahead of itself, but the tools are still handy. I'd post something about how we should be talking about wages and housing instead of robots. At work I'd keep showing Sofia the shortcuts I find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's fine for me. Hybrid work keeps growing whatever AI does, and Sofia's busy. If the robots never come, I'm a junior at a garage that's busier every year, and I can live with that. The only thing that worries me is money until Inês qualifies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with Sofia, take the higher-voltage electric course she's offered to pay for, and keep my savings habit of about a hundred and twenty a month. I'd carry on using the AI tools to learn faster. Maybe I'd start doing a bit of hybrid diagnostics on my own time to get my hands quicker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Bit of a let-down, because I like new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned money until Inês qualifies. How tight is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's fine, but there's no slack. If the car I borrow from my brother breaks, it's a week of pasta. In two years she'll earn more than me, and I'm already joking that I'll be her house husband.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you pick hybrids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because nobody else wanted them, and I like a puzzle. An old-school mechanic sees orange cables and backs away. I see job security.

say: I'd say the hype **got ahead of itself**, but the tools stay useful.
I'd steer talk back to **wages and housing** instead of robots.
think: I feel safe at a garage where **hybrid work** keeps growing.
The only strain is being **the main wage** while Inês trains.
do: Take the **higher-voltage electric** course Sofia has offered to pay for.
Keep saving about **a hundred and twenty** a month and practise diagnostics.
feel: Feels **calm**, with a small let-down because he enjoys new technology.
S0.quote: If the robots never come, I'm a junior at a garage that's busier every year, and I can live with that.
fieldNote: He chose **hybrids** deliberately as the work others avoid.
His hands are slow, but he uses **AI daily** to learn faster.
Money is tight while he's the **main earner**, but he sees an end to it.

steps.text: Take the high-voltage electric course Sofia will pay for
Save about a hundred and twenty a month
Keep working hybrids at Greenway Garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is great for small garages if the gains get shared, and terrible if they don't. AI doing the booking, the parts ordering and the quotes saves Sofia hours. I'd be online pushing for free public courses so every mechanic can use it, not just the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I come out okay, because I'm the one who already uses it. The risk is more for the older mechanics who won't touch it, and for the receptionist-type jobs. I'm a bad mechanic with a good laptop, and for a few years that might be exactly what a garage needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to set up Sofia's booking and parts system with AI in the first three months, and ask for a small raise if it saves her money. I'd use the saved hours to get proper hands-on practice with Ali, our senior. And I'd join the regional mechanics' network to share what works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit guilty. Some of what I'm excited about is what costs other people their jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ali, actually, our senior. He's brilliant with his hands but he won't go near the laptop, and Sofia might start leaning on me for diagnostics because the AI does the thinking. I'd want to teach him, not replace him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd ask for a raise. What if Sofia says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd still do it, because it's good for the garage and for my CV. But I'd keep a note of what it saved her. If there's no raise in a year, I'd show that list to other garages.

say: I'd say AI helps **small garages** only if the gains get shared.
I'd push online for **free public courses** for every mechanic.
think: I'd come out okay as the one who **already uses AI**.
Older mechanics and **front-desk jobs** carry the real risk.
do: Set up Sofia's **booking and parts** system with AI in three months.
Ask for **a raise** tied to the hours the system saves.
Spend saved hours on **hands-on practice** with Ali.
feel: Feels **excited** and a bit **guilty**, because the gains may cost others jobs.
S1.quote: I'm a bad mechanic with a good laptop, and for a few years that might be exactly what a garage needs.
fieldNote: He calls himself a **bad mechanic** with a **good laptop**, with humour and honesty.
His guilt about **Ali**, the senior, shows his progressive streak.
He'd use the change to **bargain**, keeping a record of the savings he made.

steps.text: Set up AI booking and parts ordering for Sofia

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need an emergency plan, like in a pandemic, with income support while people retrain. I'd post a lot, probably too much. At work I'd tell Sofia we've got three years before the robots, so let's think about what the garage becomes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the laptop advantage I have disappears in 2028, because the AI does the thinking for everyone. Then I'm a slow pair of hands until 2031. My one edge was being good with AI, and in two years everybody has an AI better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Sofia whether the garage could become the local place that looks after the robots and the new kit, and I'd get every certificate I could for that. I'd save harder, two hundred a month, and push Inês to finish nursing, because care might be the safer job. I'd join whatever campaign is pushing for a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be doing things to keep the fear down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Inês?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That her job might end up paying the rent, and that's fine with me. She'd laugh and say she always knew. We'd agree to hold off on getting a dog.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound like you have a plan. Would it work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a third of it. The robot servicing idea depends on companies letting small garages near their machines. I've no idea if they would.

say: I'd call for an **emergency plan** with income support during retraining.
I'd tell Sofia we have **three years** to decide what the garage becomes.
think: My **AI advantage** vanishes in 2028 when everyone has better AI.
I'd be a **slow pair of hands** until robots arrive in 2031.
do: Pitch Sofia on servicing **robots and new kit**, and gather certificates for it.
Raise savings to **two hundred** a month.
feel: Feels **anxious** but busy, doing things to keep fear down.
S2.quote: My one edge was being good with AI, and in two years everybody has an AI better than me.
fieldNote: He clearly sees his **edge disappear** when AI becomes universal.
He thinks Inês's **nursing career** may carry the household.
He doubts his **robot servicing** plan, giving it a third chance of working.

steps.text: Pitch Sofia on servicing robots and new workshop kit
Collect robot and electric system certificates
Raise savings to two hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is our chance to make it fair, with public training and some ownership for workers. I'd talk about co-ops a lot. At work I'd suggest we plan for 2031 and 2034 on the whiteboard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means I could actually get good with my hands before 2034, and that's eight years. Eight years is enough to go from bad mechanic to good one, but the robots might still be better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the electric course and a robotics maintenance short course. I'd try to persuade Sofia to make Greenway a co-op, with Ali and me owning a share, so whatever replaces us pays us too. Savings to three months, and I'd teach Ali the AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful but realistic. I'd be busy, which is how I cope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if the garage buys a robot, I want the robot's wages to come to us. Sofia's sympathetic, she's talked about retiring early. It's a long shot but not crazy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op doesn't happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd look at the big fleet depots, the delivery and taxi firms. They'll need people to keep robot-driven vans running for a while.

say: I'd argue **five years** is a chance for public training and worker ownership.
I'd suggest we **plan the garage** for 2031 and 2034 on the whiteboard.
think: I'd have **eight years** to become a good mechanic before robots arrive.
Even then, the **robots** might still be better than me.
do: Do the **electric course** and a robotics maintenance course in year one.
Propose turning Greenway into a **co-op** with Ali and me as owners.
Teach Ali the **AI tools** and grow savings to three months.
feel: Feels **hopeful but realistic**, coping by staying busy.
S3.quote: Eight years is enough to go from bad mechanic to good one, but the robots might still be better.
fieldNote: He wants workers to **own the machines** that replace them, through a co-op.
His backup is **fleet depots**, which shows he thinks several moves ahead.
He still expects his **hands-on job** to be at risk by 2034.

steps.text: Do the electric course and a robotics maintenance course
Propose making Greenway Garage a worker co-op
Apply to fleet depots if the co-op fails
Grow savings to three months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to do it right, so let's build training and worker ownership now. I'd be the guy at the pub explaining it with diagrams. At work I'd keep pushing the co-op idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is a lot for me. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, good at hybrids, maybe a part-owner. With ten years warning, I'd rather be the person who fixes the robots than the person they replace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the electric and robotics courses over two or three years, without rushing. I'd keep saving, and once Inês is earning we'd save more. I'd test any new AI tools at Greenway first and push the co-op slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Exciting, with a bit of worry for people who can't adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are those people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad, for one. He drives a bin lorry and swears at his phone. I'd want help for him, not lectures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your first co-op payout?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off Inês's student loan, or most of it. And maybe the dog.

say: I'd say **a decade** is time to build training and worker ownership properly.
I'd keep pushing the **co-op idea** at work.
think: By 2036 I'd be skilled with hybrids and maybe **a part-owner**.
I'd rather **fix the robots** than be replaced by them.
do: Take **electric and robotics** courses over two or three years.
Save more once **Inês is earning** and test new tools at Greenway.
Push the **co-op** idea slowly with Sofia and Ali.
feel: Feels **excited**, with some worry for people who **can't adapt**.

fieldNote: The long warning suits his **adaptive** nature, and he sounds energised.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my one edge disappears overnight. What would help is income support while people retrain, and ways for workers to own a share of the machines. Also some honesty from companies about what they're planning.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about people like my dad. People my age will figure something out, but nobody is helping the fifty-year-olds who swear at their phones.
